intro: A serious C-minor phrase is interrupted by lighter wind replies. Richard Penrose Arnold’s conversation becomes a musical alternation between weight and wit.
question: How can one variation keep changing the tone of a conversation?

sections.label: Lighter replies
sections.mNote: the major mode and wind figures alter the tone

sections.label: Link towards Ysobel
sections.mNote: quiet chromatic motion prepares the next portrait

cues.title: A sustained lower line
cues.text: The opening pairs a sustained lower melody with more mobile violin writing. Listen for the difference between the line’s long notes and the accompaniment’s smaller movements.
cues.evidence: Novello p. 24: the lower strings carry the sustained theme beneath violin figuration. Opening-span description.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Richard Penrose Arnold
cues.text: Richard Penrose Arnold, son of the poet Matthew Arnold, is an amateur pianist. Elgar remembers serious conversation interrupted by witty remarks; the variation’s contrasts turn that social rhythm into music.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society identifies Arnold; Elgar’s commentary describes conversation and light-hearted wind writing. https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations

cues.title: Weight and lightness alternate
cues.text: Across this portrait, keep the sustained phrase distinct from the lighter replies. A change of instrumental texture can alter the tone of a conversation without requiring a wholly unrelated theme.
cues.evidence: The Novello score and Elgar’s commentary describe minor-key seriousness and major-key wind replies. This is a whole-variation comparison, not an entrance at 1:12.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A link rather than a stop
cues.text: The ending reduces the weight and keeps a small pattern moving towards the next variation. The score asks for “attacca”: Arnold’s portrait is not designed to be sealed off by a long pause.
cues.evidence: Novello pp. 29–30 show the chromatic link and attacca marking. The report changes at 1:38 and remains comparatively quiet to the end; this source splits the next variation into another file.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The conversation changes its tone
transitions.how: C minor gives way to a lighter major-key exchange. The long line yields attention to shorter wind figures, making the contrast a change of conversational pace and colour rather than a different tempo marking.
transitions.evidence: The report changes at 0:32 and becomes quieter around 0:35. The score and Elgar’s commentary supply the change from serious minor material to light wind replies; the boundary is approximate.

transitions.title: The fragments become a connection
transitions.how: The final exchanges diminish into a quiet chromatic link. Small string figures continue under soft wind and low-brass support; the written attacca carries this preparation into Ysobel instead of adding a separate closing cadence.
transitions.evidence: Novello pp. 29–30. The report’s strongest boundary is 1:38, followed by quieter windows; this is a passage-level estimate of the written link.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: PDF pp. 24–30, rehearsal figures 15–18. Whole-variation passage map uses the report’s 0:32, 0:48, 1:24 and 1:38 changes to distinguish sustained phrases, wind replies and the final link.

timeline.note: The sustained lower-string line sits below violin figuration; bassoons and, later in the phrase, horns support it (p. 24).
The lighter exchange brings short wind figures to the foreground over reduced string support (pp. 25–26).
The larger sustained phrase is reinforced by wind and brass while the string accompaniment continues moving (pp. 26–28).
Short wind replies regain attention as the heavier texture subsides (pp. 28–29).
The chromatic closing link combines moving string figures with soft wind, low-brass and timpani support; these desks enter successively (pp. 29–30).

facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.
composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
